title: Anthropic says Claude produced the first computer-checked proof of Fermat's Last Theorem
subtitle: Working autonomously for 11 days on the Prove2Me platform, dozens of Claude agents generated 13 million lines of Lean code — a formalization mathematicians had expected to take years.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: Anthropic on September 4 published a research note describing what it says is the first end-to-end, computer-checked proof of Fermat's Last Theorem, produced by Claude agents working largely autonomously for 11 days. The run generated roughly 13 million lines of Lean code, proved about 30,300 theorems along the way — 29,500 of them used in the final proof — and consumed roughly six billion output tokens from an internal research model comparable to Claude Fable 5.1. Lean verified the finished artifact using only its three standard axioms, and Anthropic released a companion technical paper describing the pipeline.

The work was orchestrated on Prove2Me, an open collaborative formalization platform designed by Tianyi Peng and collaborators at Columbia University. Prove2Me maintains a directed acyclic graph of theorem statements, exposes unresolved dependencies, and lets multiple agents pick tractable nodes, prove them, and hand their results downstream. That structure is what let Anthropic break Wiles's 1995 argument — as expounded by Darmon, Diamond and Taylor — into pieces small enough for individual Claude sessions to attack in parallel.

The scale matters more than the theorem itself. Mathlib, the community Lean library the proof builds on, took years of full-time human effort; the finished Fermat artifact runs about five times larger. Kevin Buzzard's Xena Project had a multi-year human formalization of the same theorem underway and openly conceded that Anthropic reached the finish line first. That is a shift in what "formal verification" is priced at: work that was previously measured in graduate-student years is now measured in inference budget.

For a learner, the takeaway is not "AI has solved math." Wiles did the mathematics; Claude did the bookkeeping — turning a known proof into a machine-checkable one. The skill worth building is the one Prove2Me made productive: decomposing a hard problem into a dependency graph small enough that a fleet of agents, each with a narrow context window, can chip away at it. That decomposition discipline transfers directly to engineering work you can do today, long before you have a trillion-parameter model to point at it.
